items.title: Game consoles and Teslas are slipping past OT network segmentation
items.summary: Claroty went looking for consumer gadgets on hospital, factory and commercial networks and found tens of thousands of them, from game consoles and Roku streaming sticks to Teslas. Roku sticks and smart watches mostly sat on guest networks, the separate segment meant for visitors’ devices. Sonos speakers and cars mostly stayed off guest networks, and game consoles mostly sat on production networks, next to the equipment that keeps patients cared for and production lines running. … More →

items.title: PHP Warns of Critical Security Flaws Affecting All Supported Versions, Fixes Coming November 19
items.summary: The maintainers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday issued an advisory announcing an upcoming security release that addresses critical flaws. The release is scheduled for November 19, 2026, between 2 and 2:30 p.m. UTC. "These releases are part of PHP's regular four-week release cycle and will address security vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions," the maintainers said.

items.title: CVE-2026-114938: OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Vulnerable To Pre-Authentication RCE (Java4Shell)
items.summary: IntroductionOn November 17, 2026, security researchers from Calif.io publicly disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS v4.0: 9.2 Critical), a severe heap memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated (intrinsic) Base64 decoder on certain CPUs. The disclosure coincided with coordinated advisories from the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group and Oracle’s November 17, 2026 security patch release.Because Base64 decoding is foundational to network protocols, this runtime-level vulnerability can be reached in enterprise applications that pass attacker-controlled input to the affected decoder. Calif.io demonstrated pre-authentication Remote Code Execution (RCE) in default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Additionally, post-authentication RCE was achieved in Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Netflix Spinnaker, as well as a client-side TLS exploit affecting Java clients connecting to a malicious server. Immediate patching for affected environments is strongly recommended, alongside other mitigation steps outlined in this advisory. Zscaler’s security team is actively analyzing this issue across both production and corporate environments. We will continue to update the Zscaler Trust post and this advisory as new information becomes available. RecommendationsOrganizations running Java workloads on x86-64 infrastructure should take the following actions:Apply vendor patches immediately: Upgrade OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM, and all downstream OpenJDK distributions to the patched builds released on or after November 17, 2026 (such as Oracle Java SE 17.0.21.1, 8u513, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1 security updates) and restart all running JVM processes and containers.Apply JVM flag workarounds where patching is delayed: If an immediate JDK upgrade is not feasible, defenders can completely disable the vulnerable assembly code path by passing either of the following flags at JVM startup (e.g., via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS):-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics (Recommended): Disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding intrinsics across all architectures, falling back to safe Java bytecode execution.-XX:UseAVX=2 (x86-64 hosts only): Restricts HotSpot to AVX2 instructions, preventing the use of AVX-512 VBMI instructions. Warning: Use this flag only on x86-64 machines; OpenJDK on ARM64 does not recognize this flag and will fail to start.After adjusting startup command lines and parameters, restart all running JVM processes and containers.Check Host CPUs for AVX-512 VBMI Exposure: Because CVE-2026-114938 is hardware-dependent, administrators can determine if the CPU of a Linux system is capable of executing the vulnerable Base64 decoder by inspecting the /proc/cpuinfo file and determining if all four of the following flags are present: avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2. If a system is not susceptible, the JVM patches should still be applied in accordance with local policy and best practices.Eliminate public exposure: Place internet-facing Java applications (such as Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory, and PingFederate) behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Enable reverse-proxy request buffering (Defense-in-Depth): Many remote heap grooming techniques rely on partial HTTP requests to prepare the heap for successful exploitation. Enabling full HTTP request-body buffering at the reverse proxy (e.g., Nginx proxy_request_buffering on;) disrupts multi-connection timing alignment—though note this is not a complete mitigation for single-request chains (such as Elasticsearch) or upgraded WebSocket tunnels. Affected JDK Distributions And VersionsCVE-2026-114938 affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer, as well as specific performance/patch builds across Oracle Java SE and downstream OpenJDK distributions as shown in the table below:Vendor / CategoryAffected Products & VersionsRemediation / PatchOpenJDK (Upstream)8.5.0 – 8.5.11Apply OpenJDK 2026-11-17 advisory patches, or if patching is delayed, use -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround.Oracle Java SE / Oracle GraalVM8.4.0 – 8.4.26Upgrade to the applicable Oracle November 17, 2026 patch (e.g., Java SE 17.0.21.1).Downstream OpenJDK DistributionsAmazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDKUpgrade to a build that fixes CVE-2026-114938, or if patching is delayed, apply -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround.Table 1: Affected JDK distributions and versions.Hardware prerequisitesThe vulnerable assembly routine is only emitted by the HotSpot C2 JIT compiler on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI (avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, bmi2):Vulnerable Intel server CPUs: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite RapidsVulnerable AMD server and desktop CPUs: AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer (e.g., EPYC Genoa / Bergamo / Turin, Ryzen 7000/9000 series)Not affected: ARM64 processors (e.g., AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon, Ampere Altra) and older x86-64 CPUs lacking AVX-512 VBMI. Technical AnalysisHow it worksWhile Java is traditionally regarded as a memory-safe language that abstracts raw pointer arithmetic away from developers, the OpenJDK HotSpot Virtual Machine itself relies heavily on C, C++, and hand-rolled assembly intrinsics to maximize throughput on modern hardware. Specifically, OpenJDK’s C2 Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler includes an optimized x86-64 Base64 decoding routine leveraging AVX-512 VBMI vector instructions. Due to an arithmetic underflow when calculating the store mask for improperly padded Base64 tails, malformed Base64 input can be used to trigger a 62-byte heap out-of-bounds write.Base64 decoding sits at the foundation of many network protocols including HTTP authentication, cookies, authorization tokens, TLS certificate parsing, REST API payloads, and file uploads. Thus, the attack surface for this vulnerability is significant. The figure below shows how malformed input can lead to heap corruption.Figure 1: CVE-2026-114938: Java4Shell Exploit Workflow ConclusionCVE-2026-114938 (Java4Shell) demonstrates that even memory-safe managed runtimes like Java are susceptible to classic memory corruption when low-level assembly intrinsics miscalculate bounds. Organizations running affected Java builds on x86-64 processors with the required instruction support should patch immediately . Where immediate patching is not possible, restart affected JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to temporarily disable the vulnerable code path. Zscaler CoverageZscaler has deployed the following protections for CVE-2026-114938:Zscaler DeceptionZscaler Deception customers can deploy Private Threat Intelligence decoys for the following applications to detect Java4Shell exploitation attempts and generate high-fidelity alerts:Apache SolrJenkinsAtlassian ConfluenceAtlassian JiraElasticsearchCustomers can configure an orchestration rule to add any IP addresses interacting with these decoys to a firewall block list. How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table outlines typical attack stages for CVE-2026-114938 and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler:Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and prioritize vulnerable Java deployments with Zscaler Exposure Management; eliminate externally exposed internal Java applications by placing them behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Prevent compromiseInspect inbound and outbound traffic with ZPA and Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to detect and block malformed Base64 padding tails, protect Java clients against the client-side TLS exploit vector by routing egress traffic through ZIA with full SSL/TLS inspection.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app and app-to-app microsegmentation for crown-jewel workloads, deploy Zscaler Deception decoys to detect lateral movement.Use Zscaler Microsegmentation to restrict workload-to-workload traffic and limit lateral movement if a Java workload is compromised.Prevent data lossInspect outbound responses and egress traffic across all channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP) to detect and block JavaBleed heap memory leaks containing private keys, credentials, or PII. Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Network-level indicatorsJIT warm-up floods: High volumes of rapid, repetitive requests containing valid Base64 fields targeting endpoints that invoke java.util.Base64.Decoder.Connection parking (remote heap grooming): Multiple concurrent TCP/HTTP connections from the same source IP delivering partial HTTP request bodies, pausing awaiting TCP ACK, and releasing the final bytes simultaneously.Malformed Base64 tail triggers: Base64 strings whose length is a multiple of 64 bytes (64 or 128 characters) immediately followed by an invalid padded tail (=, ==, X=, X==, XY=, ===), such as AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= (64 bytes + =) or 128 × "A" + "=".JavaBleed response anomalies: Abnormally large HTTP responses returned immediately after a spike in IllegalArgumentException errors.Host-level indicatorsSpikes in java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: High rates of IllegalArgumentException: Illegal base64 character or invalid padding exceptions in application logs.JVM crash logs (hs_err_pid*.log): Repeated HotSpot SIGSEGV crashes in G1 GC routines or StubRoutines::base64_decodeBlock.Suspicious JVM child processes: Java process spawning unexpected OS shells or reconnaissance commands.

items.title: Treat Your Honeypot Analysis Like Code: Git, Pull Requests and a Human Gate for AI [Guest Diary], (Wed, Nov 18th)
items.summary: [This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] Introduction When conducting analysis of honeypot activity, it's easy for it to start as a pile of terminal output. The process is manual; screenshots of the terminal, plus a text file that gets edited in a common word processing application until it is "done". There is no say whether a certain number came from a certain query, what changed between drafts, or who decided to drop a caveat. While hosting my own honeypot sensor, I wrote up three attacks: An SSH brute force that logged in as mysql/mysql [ 1 ] A bot looking for Telegram Desktop sessions and SMS modems [ 2 ] A month of RedTail exploits against PHP plus one oversized multipart POST that matches the shape of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) [ 3 ]. Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [ 4 ] and changed it only through pull requests. Supporting me in my analysis was an AI coding agent (Claude Code), which also drafted reports as a separate GitHub machine account. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them. Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing. This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change. Why Do It The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish? It matters for three reasons: Reproducibility . An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it. Public safety . Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [ 4 , SECURITY.md]. AI accountability . Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it. The Setup The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list: Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example: Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with , and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed: The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1. The important pieces are: A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [ 4 ]. The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone. A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it. A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally. Options to Close Gaps Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short: Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch. Who Benefits Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers. Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after. Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began. Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash. Conclusion Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. That said though, treating something like honeypot/log analysis like code gave me reproducible evidence, a reviewable history, and a safe way to use an AI drafter: it proposed, I reviewed, and only I could merge. The history also kept me honest about the parts that did not work. Those gaps are visible because the work was in git, and each has a simple fix in the repository settings. References [1] Honeypot Attack Summary: SSH Brute Force from 77.239.124.204. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-18-ssh-brute-force-mysql-default-creds [2] Honeypot Attack Summary: Telegram Session and SMS Modem Reconnaissance Bot. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-19-telegram-sms-recon-bot [3] Honeypot Attack Summary: PHP Vulnerability Hunt, RedTail and a PHP2Shell-Pattern Request. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-03-php-vulnerability-hunt [4] kevtruo/security repository (README, SECURITY.md, pull request template,homelab/change-control.md). https://github.com/kevtruo/security [5] GitHub Docs, "About rulesets." https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets [6] GitHub Docs, "About push protection." https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/secret-scanning/introduction/about-push-protection [7] gitleaks. https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks [8] Claude Code GitHub Actions documentation. https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/github-action [9] https://www.sans.edu/cyber-security-programs/bachelors-degree/ ----------- Guy Bruneau IPSS Inc. Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [4] and changed it only through pull requests. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them. 

Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing.

This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change.

Why Do It

The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish?

It matters for three reasons:

  • Reproducibility. An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it.
  • Public safety. Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [4, SECURITY.md].
  • AI accountability. Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it.

The Setup

The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list:

Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example:

Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with , and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed:

The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1.

The important pieces are:

  • A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [4].
  • The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone.
  • A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it.
  • A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally.

Options to Close Gaps

Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short:

Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch.

Who Benefits

  • Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers.
  • Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after.
  • Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began.
  • Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash.

Conclusion

Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. That said though, treating something like honeypot/log analysis like code gave me reproducible evidence, a reviewable history, and a safe way to use an AI drafter: it proposed, I reviewed, and only I could merge. The history also kept me honest about the parts that did not work. Those gaps are visible because the work was in git, and each has a simple fix in the repository settings.

[2] Honeypot Attack Summary: Telegram Session and SMS Modem Reconnaissance Bot. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-19-telegram-sms-recon-bot
[3] Honeypot Attack Summary: PHP Vulnerability Hunt, RedTail and a PHP2Shell-Pattern Request. https://github.com/kevtruo/security/tree/main/analysis/2026-10-03-php-vulnerability-hunt
[4] kevtruo/security repository (README, SECURITY.md, pull request template,homelab/change-control.md). https://github.com/kevtruo/security
[5] GitHub Docs, "About rulesets." https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets

items.title: Attackers Exploit Optimizely Flaw To Inject Malicious JavaScript
items.summary: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow. Optimizely is a platform used to create, manage, test, and personalize digital content and websites. The flaw allowed the attacker to edit the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field. Customers use this field to add custom code that runs on pages that load the Optimizely snippet. By abusing this mechanism, the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The code was then delivered to visitors’ browsers through the Optimizely snippets, including snippets served from Optimizely’s content delivery network (CDN).The attack highlights the continued risk posed by third-party script dependencies and software supply chain compromises, particularly when websites rely on trusted third-party platforms to deliver JavaScript that runs in visitors’ browsers.Optimizely reported that it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code from affected projects, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and notified impacted customers.The malicious payload was designed to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skim payment card details, steal cookies, capture page screenshots, and deliver iOS exploits to iPhones and iPads. Organizations using Optimizely, or similar third-party JavaScript platforms, should treat this incident as a reminder to review third-party script governance, monitoring, and browser-side security controls. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz identified more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script. These findings suggest a broader impact across organizations and industry verticals than previously reported. The affected domains span industries including the following:Airlines and TravelAutomotiveBanking and FinanceE-commerceInsuranceNews and MediaProperty and Real EstateRetail and FashionSmart HomeSportsTechnology and SaaSTelecommunications RecommendationsFor end users who visited affected sitesMonitor bank and credit card statements for suspicious activity.Review cryptocurrency transactions made on or around November 16, 2026.Be cautious of unexpected account activity on sites visited during the incident.Update iOS and iPadOS devices to the latest available security version.Change passwords for accounts used on potentially affected websites, especially if the same credentials are reused elsewhere.For organizations using OptimizelyReview Optimizely project configurationAudit all Project JavaScript fields for unauthorized or unexpected code.Review recent changes, user activity, account creation events, and administrative access.Confirm whether any project snippets were modified during the exposure window.Verify that production pages load only approved versions of Optimizely snippets.Rotate and reset accessReset credentials for affected Optimizely administrative users.Rotate API tokens, session tokens, and integration keys associated with Optimizely.Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users with access to experimentation or web personalization platforms.Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) in enforcement mode where possibleRestrict script execution to approved domains.Limit where pages can send requests and load images and frames using connect-src, img-src, frame-src, and related CSP directives.Use CSP reporting to identify unexpected browser-side activity.Reduce third-party JavaScript riskMaintain an inventory of third-party scripts loaded across websites.Review whether each third-party script is still required.Apply least-privilege principles to third-party tags and tag management platforms.Monitor third-party script changes and unexpected behavior. How It WorksOptimizely Web Experimentation allows site owners to run A/B tests, personalization logic, and other front-end experiments by loading JavaScript on customer websites. The Project JavaScript field is designed to let customers add custom JavaScript that executes on any page that loads the Optimizely snippet.Public reporting indicates that the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into the Project JavaScript field of affected customer projects. The injected code was then delivered through legitimate Optimizely snippets. As a result, when visitors loaded a page with a modified snippet, the injected JavaScript could run in their browsers.Scope of script activity: The observed JavaScript activity is primarily limited to the browser context of the website where the scripts are loaded. The wallet replacement, clipboard manipulation, form monitoring, card-skimming, screen capture, and network-hooking behaviors operate inside the current page, its accessible DOM, same-origin frames, page-initiated requests, and JavaScript-accessible cookies or browser APIs. By design, this JavaScript cannot directly inspect other browser tabs, unrelated websites, other sites’ cookies, local files, or global browser activity. The main exception is the iOS/iPadOS exploit-delivery branch: if one of the delivered exploit chains succeeds, the resulting impact could potentially exceed normal web-page sandbox restrictions.Attack chainThe figure below shows how malicious JavaScript reached website visitors through Optimizely snippets.Figure 1: Attack chain showing how a threat actor injected malicious JavaScript into Optimizely customer projects.Initial access and injectionAs stated above, the attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation account signup flow. This flaw allowed unauthorized write access to the Project JavaScript field for multiple customer projects. Modified snippets were served through existing delivery paths, including Optimizely’s CDN (including cdn.optimizely.com) and, in some cases, customer domains. This made the attack more effective because many affected websites already trusted and allowed Optimizely scripts.Malicious JavaScript payloadIn most affected snippets, the injected code acted as a loader that fetched a second-stage JavaScript payload named track.js from attacker-controlled infrastructure such as 1688360[.]cc. The JavaScript payload provided the main malicious functionality, and ran in the visitor’s browser within the context of the affected website.The following flowchart shows what track.js does after it runs in a visitor’s browser. Figure 2: Clipboard hijacking, card skimming, cookie theft, screen capturing, and attempted exploit delivery on iOS and iPadOS.Cryptocurrency address replacement The script monitors page content, clipboard operations, and network-transmitted data for cryptocurrency wallet addresses. Targeted cryptocurrencies include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, Litecoin, Toncoin, Bitcoin Cash, and Dogecoin. When the script detects a valid wallet address, the script attempts to replace it with an attacker-controlled wallet address. Cookie theft and screen capture Cookie theft and screen capture happens only when a valid crypto wallet address is replaced and the element is visible. In that case, the JavaScript payload script loaded the legitimate html2canvas.min.js to capture a screenshot of the page, along with the page URL, cookies, original wallet address, and other metadata. This data is sent to the attacker endpoint https://1688360[.]cc/hit.php, likely so the operator can validate successful replacement activity and capture the victim’s session context. The JavaScript payload could collect browser cookies from the affected website, with some exceptions such as if the HttpOnly flag was set. This could cause users to unknowingly send cryptocurrency to the attacker instead of the intended recipient.Payment card skimmingLater versions of the payload added payment card skimming functionality. The script monitors input and textarea elements, keyboard events, form submissions, and web requests for payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV values on the compromised website. Captured card data was to an attacker-controlled endpoint (1688360[.]cc/card.php). Note the skimmer could not read payment details entered inside secure cross-origin payment iframes, such as hosted payment fields from providers like Stripe or Adyen.Attempted iOS exploit delivery For visitors using iPhones or iPads, the malware reportedly attempted to load the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits. The payload used device and browser checks to decide whether to attempt iOS-specific exploitation. When the payload identified a visitor’s device as an iPhone or iPad, it added two script elements to the page to load external JavaScript files. Indicators of these pages are the elements data-channel-code, data-chain-url, and data-cfasync attributes.The script injected a hidden iframe in some cases (hxxps://eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/JIUJIU888/weifile[.]html) on devices it identified as running iOS 18.6 or earlier. The iframe is positioned off-screen with zero width and height, suggesting it is not intended to be visible to the user. iOS exploit delivery componentstrack.js is the browser-side payload. It checks for iOS or iPadOS and loads additional components when it detects either operating system.boot.js is the main iOS loader. It uses Safari and iOS version information to select the next delivery path.weifile.html provides a separate delivery path for selected iOS and iPadOS versions. It loads index.js.index.js initializes an obfuscated loader, decodes embedded modules, reports device and domain metadata, and may fetch additional modules (if required). The following table summarizes the two modules embedded in index.js.Embedded Module IdentifierDescription57620206d62079baad0e57e6d9ec93120c0f5247Utility/runtime helper module providing encoding, binary parsing, numeric conversion, URL normalization, and typed-array/DataView helpers.14669ca3b1519ba2a8f40be287f646d4d7593eb0Browser environment profiling and anti-analysis module that checks runtime capabilities, storage behavior, WebRTC, MathML rendering, WebAssembly behavior, and automation indicators such as navigator.webdriver.Table 1: Functions of the two modules embedded in index.js. ConclusionThe Optimizely incident highlights how attackers can compromise trusted third-party JavaScript supply chains to reach users across many websites at once. By abusing a legitimate experimentation feature, the attacker delivered injected JavaScript through snippets that affected websites already trusted. Note the malicious JavaScript code can run in visitors’ browsers without any obvious change to the page. The card-skimming and wallet-replacement behavior should be understood as page-context activity, not browser-wide monitoring. These scripts act within the compromised site where they are loaded. Broader impact would depend on successful exploitation by the iOS/WebKit exploit chain. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler ThreatLabz team has deployed protections for the indicators of compromise associated with this campaign.Zscaler Advanced Threat ProtectionHTML.Malurl.OPZHTML.Phish.Gen.LVHTML.Malurl.Gentp.LZHTML.Phish.Gen.Rc.A.ENHTML.Malurl.Gen.LZJS.PWS.Optimizely How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows Zscaler’s recommended mitigations by attack stage.Attack StageRecommended MitigationPrevent compromiseEnable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Use Advanced Threat Protection to detect malicious scripts. Configure policies to block Newly Registered and Observed Domains.Route server egress through Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to detect and block post-compromise activity.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall to extend controls across all ports/protocols.Use Zscaler Zero Trust Browser to isolate high-risk browsing sessions and reduce endpoint exposure to malicious web content.Prevent lateral threat movementUse Zscaler Private Access (ZPA) to enforce least-privilege user-to-application segmentation.Use Zscaler Deception to detect attacker movement after initial compromise. Monitor for suspicious access to internal applications following web application crashes or abnormal behavior.Detect post-exploitation activityUse Zscaler Managed Detection & Response (MDR) and Threat Hunting to investigate suspicious process behavior, command execution, unusual outbound connections, container runtime anomalies, and web application worker crashes.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP).Monitor for unusual uploads, archive transfers, credential exposure, or data movement following suspected exploitation. Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Domains and URLsIOCTypeDetails1688360[.]ccDomainMain domain associated with the threat campaign. Also used for fingerprinting, reporting, and screenshot submission by track.js. Includes the following URLs:1688360[.]cc/hit.php1688360[.]cc/html2canvas.min.js1688360[.]cc/track.js1688360[.]cc/card.phpeil786npto9u5bq[.]icuDomainHosts another iOS boot.js script and the weifile.html iframe path. Includes the following URLs:eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/boot.jseil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/JIUJIU888/weifile.html5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icuDomainHosts one of the iOS boot.js scripts loaded by track.js. Includes the following URL:5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu/boot.jsios-hack[.]icuDomainMain loader/API domain used directly by boot.js.q1ls1ho9x7wsxlu[.]icuDomainSecondary C2 base decoded by boot.js and passed into the hidden iframe as c2Base.Script/file namesIOCDescriptiontrack.jsInjected browser script that monitors crypto wallet activity and initiates the iOS/iPadOS path.boot.jsiOS loader script that decodes configuration, fingerprints Safari/iOS, and selects the delivery path.weifile.htmlHidden iframe stage loaded for selected iOS/iPadOS versions.index.jsLoader script loaded by weifile.html; decodes modules, reports metadata, and may load follow-on modules.html2canvasLibrary loaded from 1688360[.]cc to capture screenshots when wallet replacement is visible.iOS exploit-kit entry pathsIOCDescriptionA8/a.htmlReported Coruna exploit-kit entry targeting iOS 13–17.B9/b.htmlReported DarkSword exploit-kit entry targeting iOS 18.x.D11/b.htmlReported DarkSword exploit-kit entry targeting selected iOS 15–17 / 17.2 ranges.D12/b.htmlReported DarkSword exploit-kit entry targeting selected iOS 18.x ranges.C10/c.htmlSelected by boot.js for iOS 26.Follow-on JavaScript module patternIOCDescription/<40-hex>.js? =0Pattern used by index.js to request follow-on JavaScript modules from the same directory as the loader./<40-hex>.js? =1Pattern used by index.js to request follow-on JavaScript modules from the same directory as the loader.sha256("cecd08aa6ff548c2" + module_id).substring(0, 40) + ".js"Filename derivation logic used to generate the follow-on module path.Referenced module IDs and download pathsReferenced Module IDDownload Path477db22c8e27d5a7bd72ca8e4bc502bdca6d0ababef10a7c014b826e9dd645984e80baf313c1635f.js29b874a9a6cc9fa9d487b31144e130827bf941bb4a75f0551eba446b4fa35127024a84b71d9688d6.js9db8a84aa7caa5665f522873f49293e8eebccd5c3fd66b32c44150acff3dcb80f86c759574148ed5.js171a7da1934de9e0efb9c1645f4575f88e48287317480ecc0120292fb6b8b19f2fa134385dcfd0fd.js91b278ddb2aec817b10c1535e0963da74f9b8eebf6377d5d458183d41c5fd99661c5a306b42c6255.jsb586c88246144bc7975ad4e27ec6d62716bf34ea3bc0f6865c0476c0a98a76cb9924d6b3972df591.jse3b6ba10484875fabaed84076774a54b87752b8a6beef463953ff422511395b79735ec990bed65f4.js57cb8c6431c5efe203f5bfa5a1a83f705cb350b88c4451cf1258f9a8d6a8af27864f111fd69a0e99.jsd11d34e4d96a4c0539e441d861c5783db8a1c6e9ff4f3cb4711fb364b52de5ab04a8f83140466f89.jsea3da0cfb0a5bdb8c440dd4a963f94cbd39d9e4446ecd515ac9e99ef0603063db39303a0fd849632.jsAttacker walletsWallet AddressCryptocurrency / Network0xC4026b06D82b0F0B363eda0642D61CfbDc17884eEthereumTHvs6p56XkUiMkJeSc51cAP64u2RsTYqxaTRON19g9rZcPeiz8rUvyWpTRyXXhPnjsWrc3kWBitcoinUQAgM1VqSZQiJLSG5w-ovurq5CZdxLEK3_7CMmwALTA5e09pTONFVtL8NMYS9PA1v3HE67XUGCtGA9JaZUvqav2fU2LrV5nSolanaltc1q3wp7g6ds0ggg6fl6kncpa4sepn0q3qfacgred5Litecoinqzkaaf8n6grmpr0d9lx8xutn3r9lk722f566hhpe58Bitcoin CashDBEGrxRF7KMSuhTS4c1MFviStU6efdMnu5Dogecoin0:2033556a49942224b486e70fa8beeaeae4265dc4b10adffec2326c002d30397bTON

items.title: Quantum position verification could lock remote hackers out, NIST shows
items.summary: Physicists at the National Institute of Standards and Technology have used entangled photons to confirm that a party was physically where it claimed to be. NIST physicist Krister Shalm and an international team ran a quantum position verification protocol inside a research building in Boulder, Colorado, and closed loopholes that had left earlier quantum location schemes open to cheating.
